parole.significato: britchka, buggy (type of horse-drawn carriage, with a foldable roof covering)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish bryczka.
Borrowed from Polish dalej (“come on!, forward!”, literally “further”).

parole.significato: an East Prussian coin worth ten pfennigs
parole.testo: Perhaps from Polish dudek (“hoopoe”), used derogatorily of the Polish three-grosz coin with an eagle on it.
ergo- + -nomie, from Polish ergonomia, coined in 1857 by Wojciech Jastrzębowski by combining Ancient Greek ἔργον (érgon) + νόμος (nómos).

parole.significato: beau, dandy, fop, peacock, pompous twit (arrogant, vain man)
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Polish Wacku, the vocative form of Wacek, which is the diminutive form of the given name Wacław, itself from Czech Václav, from Old Czech Venceslav, from Proto-Slavic *Vęťeslàvъ. Doublet of Wenzel.

parole.significato: Intensifies nouns, giving them a negative quality.
parole.testo: From Hure (“whore”), likely back-formation from Hurensohn (“son of a whore”). Possible calque of Polish kurwa (“whore, general profanity”) in some contexts.

parole.significato: a type of military jacket used by the Prussian army
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish litewka (literally “Lithuanian”), possibly via Kashubian.

Borrowed from Polish mazurek.
Borrowed from Polish młotek, introduced by Polish-speaking immigrants during the industrialisation of the Ruhrgebiet.

parole.significato: intervals, each containing a low note followed by the pitch that is one octave higher, played on a keyboard, especially…
parole.testo: From Murky + Bässe. The former word is from Polish Murcki.

parole.significato: all is not lost; hope springs eternal
parole.testo: Calque of Polish jeszcze Polska nie zginęła (“Poland is not lost yet”), a famous line from the Polish national anthem. Compare Swedish än är inte Polen förlorat.
Borrowed from Polish ogonek (literally “little tail”).
19th century, borrowed from Polish pieniądze, plural of pieniądz, from Proto-Slavic *pěnędzь, from Proto-Germanic *panningaz. Doublet of Pfennig. See English penny for more.

Older also Pippaw, at least since the 16th century, and earlier with vaguer correspondences to composite plants; from Polish pępawa or another West Slavic regiolect close to it, seemingly having a masculine by-form.
Borrowed from Polish pić + -en.

parole.significato: Pole, Polack (person from Poland, male or unspecified sex)
parole.testo: From Polish Polak (“a Polish person”).

parole.significato: an unorganized group of people, typically between ±7 and 100; a mob, but not necessarily aggressive
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish pułk, from Proto-Slavic *pъlkъ, probably from Proto-Germanic *fulką, and then a doublet of Volk.

parole.significato: a political radical, especially a fugleman or firebrand
parole.testo: Late 19th century, from radikal + -inski. The latter suffix was also used in some other formations (like Brutalinski), but Radikalinski is the commonest and perhaps original form. parole.significato: uhlan (lancer, a soldier armed with a lance in a former light cavalry unit)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish ułan, from Turkish oğlan.
From Woiwode + -schaft, after Polish województwo.
Borrowed from Polish złoty.
Either from French botte or Polish bot, in both cases ultimately from Old French bote (“boot”).

parole.significato: chamber, a room for abode mediocrely furnitured
parole.testo: Depending on the region from either Upper Sorbian komorka or Polish komórka. Doublet of Kammer and Kamera.

19th century, from East Central German dialects. Further origin uncertain. Plausibly from Polish kleć (“outhouse”), from Proto-Slavic *klětь. Alternatively from klitschen (“to splat, slap”), a variant of klatschen.

parole.significato: field pea (Pisum sativum subsp. arvense syn. Pisum sativum convar. speciosum)
parole.testo: Borrowed from either Czech peluška or Polish peluszka or Russian пелю́шка (peljúška), from Ukrainian пелю́шка (peljúška, “napkin, diaper, field pea”), from the shapes of the blossoms and leaves.
